name: Tracking Growth
title: Tracking Growth
answer: Tracking growth means watching English learners' progress in both language and content, not just one. Proficiency growth charts show whether a student is moving through English levels at a healthy pace, and a stalled flag starts a conversation with the English language development team. This matters because growth data helps teachers decide when to fade support and when to add targeted help, while teachers still make the decisions.

sections.body: The idea is to track English learners' development in two dimensions at once, language proficiency and content learning. It solves the problem of seeing only a single score or a single subject and missing whether a student is actually advancing. Proficiency growth charts give a view of whether a student is moving through English levels at a healthy pace. When a teacher charts annual proficiency scores, for example in Google Sheets, the teacher can flag students whose growth has stalled. That flag is not a verdict, it begins a conversation with the English language development team.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school, a teacher can use Google Sheets to chart annual proficiency scores and flag students whose growth has stalled, which starts a conversation with the English language development team. The text gives a grade band for one piece of evidence: a scaled literacy program redesigned for English learners in kindergarten through third grade. In that study, the largest benefits appeared for students in second and third grade who had weaker reading skills. Teachers should also check results for their own students, because a tool's average effect may hide which students it helps most. Growth data should guide the fade of support, so a student growing quickly may be ready for less translation and simpler frames, while a student whose growth has stalled may need more targeted help rather than more of the same tool.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text cites one study, Connor et al. (2022), of a scaled literacy program redesigned for English learners in kindergarten through third grade. It found mixed results overall, with the largest benefits for students in second and third grade who had weaker reading skills. The text does not give a formal evidence label for this finding. The broader point is that a tool's average effect may hide which students it helps most. Teachers should check results for their own students.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits on what data can do. A flag for stalled growth is a signal to talk with the English language development team, not an automatic placement or a substitute for professional judgment. Data informs decisions about fading support, such as reducing translation and simpler frames for a student whose English is growing quickly, or adding targeted help for a student whose growth has stalled. Teachers make those decisions. The text also warns that adaptive literacy technology can help some English learners more than others, so average results should not be applied blindly, and the decisions about support remain with people.
